title: Capstone 2 kickoff: Firebase project and authentication
goal: Start StandupBoard, a real-time team standup app, and add sign-in with Firebase Authentication.

concepts: The capstone: StandupBoard. Teams post daily updates (yesterday, today, blockers) that appear live for everyone
Firebase: a backend-as-a-service (Auth, Firestore, Hosting); the free Spark plan is enough
When to use Firebase vs your own Express + PostgreSQL (and why this project uses both)
Firebase JS SDK (modular): initializeApp, getAuth
Sign-in methods: email/password and Google; onAuthStateChanged
ID tokens: short-lived JWTs issued by Firebase

resources.title: Firebase: Add Firebase to your JavaScript project

build.task: Create a NEW repo standupboard with web/ (Angular + Tailwind) and api/ (Express + TypeScript). Write docs/product.md with 8 user stories (sign in, create a team, invite by code, post today's standup, see the team's standups live, flag blockers, admins can remove posts and members, history by date). Create a Firebase project, enable email/password and Google sign-in, and put the web config in Angular environment files. Build an AuthService with signals wrapping onAuthStateChanged, sign-up, sign-in (email and Google) and sign-out, plus login/register pages and an auth guard. Show the user's name and photo in the header.
acceptance: docs/product.md with 8 user stories and a 'not in MVP' list
Email/password and Google sign-in both work
Auth state is exposed as signals; the guard waits for the first auth state before deciding
Firebase web config in environment files (it is not secret, but service account keys are)
Header shows the signed-in user; sign-out works

hints: Wrap the callback in a signal: user = signal<User | null | undefined>(undefined); onAuthStateChanged(auth, u => this.user.set(u)). undefined means 'still checking', so the guard waits until it's no longer undefined.
Google sign-in: await signInWithPopup(auth, new GoogleAuthProvider()). Add localhost and your future domain under Authentication → Settings → Authorised domains.

The Firebase web config (apiKey and so on) identifies your project and is safe in client code. Security comes from Auth and security rules. A service account JSON is a real secret and must never go in git.

explainBack.q: The Firebase apiKey is in your frontend code. Why isn't that a security hole?
lookFor: it identifies the project, doesn't grant access
access is controlled by Auth and security rules
service account keys are the real secrets

explainBack.q: Why does the auth guard need a 'still checking' state?
lookFor: otherwise it redirects to login on reload

lastHintExplanation: The Firebase web config only tells the SDK which project to talk to. What a user can actually read or write is decided by Firebase Auth and your security rules on the server side. On reload, Firebase restores the session asynchronously, so a guard that checks immediately sees 'no user' and wrongly redirects. Waiting for the first auth event fixes that.

title: Firestore: data model and real-time listeners
goal: Model StandupBoard in Firestore and stream live updates into Angular signals.

concepts: Firestore: collections, documents, subcollections; no joins
Modelling for reads: teams/{teamId}/standups/{standupId}, members stored on the team
Denormalisation: copying the author's name and photo into each standup
addDoc, setDoc, updateDoc, serverTimestamp()
Queries: where, orderBy, limit; composite indexes
onSnapshot for real-time updates, and unsubscribing on destroy

build.task: In standupboard/web: create Firestore (test mode for today only; rules come on Day 142). Model teams/{teamId} with name, inviteCode, ownerUid and a members map { uid: { role, name, photoURL } }, and teams/{teamId}/standups/{id} with uid, authorName, yesterday, today, blockers, hasBlocker, date (YYYY-MM-DD) and createdAt (serverTimestamp). Build: create team, join by invite code, a team page with today's standups streaming live via onSnapshot into a signal (unsubscribe on destroy), a post/edit-my-standup form (one per user per day: use the doc id `${date}_${uid}`), and a date picker for past days. Open two browsers with two users and watch updates arrive live. Write docs/firestore-model.md explaining your structure and denormalisation choices.
acceptance: Teams and standups stored as described; one standup per user per day
Team page updates live in a second browser without refreshing
Listeners unsubscribe when leaving the page (no duplicate updates when returning)
Past days viewable via the date picker
docs/firestore-model.md explains the structure and why data is denormalised

hints: Live signal: const unsub = onSnapshot(query(collection(db, 'teams', teamId, 'standups'), where('date', '==', date), orderBy('createdAt')), snap => this.standups.set(snap.docs.map(d => ({ id: d.id, ...d.data() })))); inject(DestroyRef).onDestroy(unsub);
where + orderBy on different fields needs a composite index. The error message in the console contains a link that creates it for you.
Using the id `${date}_${uid}` with setDoc(..., { merge: true }) makes 'one standup per user per day' automatic: posting again just updates it.
proof: Commit with the Firestore model, team pages and docs.

explainBack.q: Why copy the author's name into each standup instead of looking it up?
lookFor: trade-off: must update copies if the name changes

explainBack.q: What happens if you forget to unsubscribe from onSnapshot?
lookFor: duplicate updates when you come back

lastHintExplanation: Firestore has no joins, so you design documents around the screens that read them. Copying the author's name into each standup makes the board a single query; the cost is updating the copies if a name changes. Every onSnapshot keeps a live connection until you call its unsubscribe function, so forgotten listeners pile up, duplicate updates and use up your free read quota.

predict.q: You call setDoc on teams/t1/standups/2026-12-01_u1 twice with different text. How many documents exist?
predict.why: A document id is unique within a collection; setDoc writes to that one document.

title: Express + Firebase Admin: verifying users and roles
goal: Connect your own Express API to Firebase users: verify ID tokens and manage roles with custom claims.

concepts: Why an Express API alongside Firebase: trusted server logic, admin tasks, integrations, reports
Firebase Admin SDK with a service account (an env var, never committed)
verifyIdToken(idToken): checks signature, expiry and project
Sending the ID token from Angular: await user.getIdToken() in an interceptor
Custom claims for roles (admin/member) and forcing a token refresh
Admin SDK writes bypass security rules, so validate carefully

resources.title: Firebase Admin: Add the SDK to your server

build.task: In standupboard/api: install firebase-admin and load credentials from a FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT env var (JSON string, validated by zod; never committed). Write requireFirebaseUser middleware (Bearer ID token → verifyIdToken → res.locals.user = { uid, email, role }; 401 otherwise). Endpoints: GET /api/me; POST /api/teams/:teamId/members/:uid/role (team owner only) that sets the role in the team's members map; GET /api/teams/:teamId/report?from=&to= that returns per-member standup counts and blocker counts (members only). In Angular, add an interceptor that attaches await auth.currentUser.getIdToken() to /api requests. Write supertest tests with verifyIdToken injected as a fake.
acceptance: Service account loaded from env; nothing secret in git
Invalid, expired or missing tokens get 401
Only the team owner can change roles (403 otherwise); non-members get 404 on the report
Angular sends a fresh ID token automatically
Tests use an injected fake verifier and cover 401, 403, 404 and success

hints: Credentials: initializeApp({ credential: cert(JSON.parse(config.FIREBASE_SERVICE_ACCOUNT)) }). In .env, put the JSON on one line in single quotes.

Interceptor with an async token: return from(auth.currentUser?.getIdToken() ?? Promise.resolve(null)).pipe(switchMap(t => next(t ? req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${t}` } }) : req))). getIdToken refreshes automatically when needed.
Make the app testable: createApp({ verifyIdToken, db }) so tests pass a fake verifier instead of calling Google.
proof: Commit with the Admin SDK setup, middleware, endpoints and tests.

explainBack.q: Why must the server verify the ID token instead of trusting a uid sent by the client?
lookFor: verification proves Firebase issued it to that user

explainBack.q: Admin SDK writes bypass security rules. What does that mean for your API code?

lastHintExplanation: Anyone can send { uid: 'someone-else' } to your API. Only a verified ID token proves Firebase signed in that user recently for your project. The Admin SDK runs with full privileges and ignores security rules, so every permission check (membership, owner-only actions) must be in your Express code, just like the user_id scoping in Phase 4.

predict.q: An admin sets a custom claim role: 'admin' on a user who is already signed in. When does their ID token include it?
options: After the token refreshes (up to an hour, or when forced with getIdToken(true))
predict.why: Claims are embedded in tokens, which refresh about hourly or when forced.

title: Security rules and role-based access
goal: Lock down Firestore with security rules so the database itself enforces who can read and write what.

concepts: Security rules: match paths, allow read/write if conditions
request.auth, resource.data (existing doc) and request.resource.data (incoming doc)
Helper functions: isSignedIn(), isMember(teamId), isAdmin(teamId) with get()
Validating fields: types, sizes, allowed keys (keys().hasOnly)
Preventing users from changing their own role
The Firebase Emulator Suite and @firebase/rules-unit-testing

resources.title: Firestore: Get started with security rules
Firestore: Writing conditions for security rules
Firebase: Test security rules with the emulator

build.task: In standupboard: write firestore.rules. Teams: members can read; signed-in users can create a team where they are the owner and an admin; only admins can update the name; nobody can change their own role through the client. Standups: members can read; a user can create or update only a standup whose id ends with their uid and whose uid field equals request.auth.uid; text fields are strings under 1,000 characters; only the listed keys are allowed; the author or a team admin can delete. Install the Firebase CLI, run the emulators, and write 12+ rules tests with @firebase/rules-unit-testing (members vs non-members, editing someone else's standup, changing your own role, oversized text). Deploy the rules and remove test mode.

starterFiles.name: firestore.rules

acceptance: Test mode removed; rules deployed
Non-members can't read a team or its standups
Users can't write standups as someone else or change their own role
Field validation: types, sizes and allowed keys
12+ passing rules tests against the emulator
The app still works for legitimate users

hints: Ownership on create: allow create: if isMember(teamId) && request.resource.data.uid == request.auth.uid && standupId.matches('.*_' + request.auth.uid);

Block role self-promotion on team updates: require request.resource.data.members[request.auth.uid].role == resource.data.members[request.auth.uid].role for non-admins, or route all role changes through your Express API and deny them in rules.
Test pattern: const alice = testEnv.authenticatedContext('alice').firestore(); await assertFails(setDoc(doc(alice, 'teams/t1/standups/2026-12-01_bob'), {...}));
proof: Commit with firestore.rules and the rules tests.

explainBack.q: Your Angular app already hides the delete button for non-admins. Why do you still need rules?
lookFor: anyone can call the SDK from the console
resource.data = the document as it is now
request.resource.data = what it would be after the write
compare them to block changes to fields

lastHintExplanation: With Firebase, the browser talks to the database directly, so anyone can open DevTools and call setDoc with any data. Security rules are the only server-side gatekeeper. resource.data is the stored document and request.resource.data is the document as it would look after the write, so comparing them lets you forbid changing particular fields, such as your own role.

predict.why: The rule only checks sign-in, not membership.

title: Real-time features: presence, reactions and offline
goal: Make StandupBoard feel alive: who's online, live reactions, a blockers panel, and graceful offline behaviour.

concepts: Presence: a lastSeen timestamp updated on an interval while the tab is visible
The Page Visibility API (document.visibilityState)
Atomic updates: increment(), arrayUnion(), arrayRemove()
Transactions and batched writes in Firestore
Offline persistence: the persistentLocalCache option; pending writes (hasPendingWrites)
Showing sync state to users

resources.title: Firestore: Add and update data (increment, arrayUnion)

build.task: In standupboard/web: presence (each member's lastSeen in teams/{teamId}/presence/{uid}, updated every 60 seconds while the tab is visible; avatars show 'online' if lastSeen is under 2 minutes ago); emoji reactions on standups using a reactions map with arrayUnion/arrayRemove of uids (toggle); a live 'Blockers today' panel with a query on hasBlocker == true; a 'Mark blocker resolved' action by the author or an admin. Enable offline persistence and show a 'Saving…/Saved/Offline' indicator using hasPendingWrites and the browser's online/offline events. Update the security rules and rules tests for presence and reactions (users may only add or remove their own uid).
acceptance: Online indicators update across browsers within about a minute
Presence pauses when the tab is hidden
Reactions toggle atomically and users can only change their own reaction
Blockers panel updates live; resolving works with the right permissions
Offline: posting works, shows 'Offline', and syncs when back online
Rules and tests updated for the new data

hints: Toggle reaction: updateDoc(ref, { [`reactions.${emoji}`]: hasReacted ? arrayRemove(uid) : arrayUnion(uid) }). Concurrent reactions from different users won't overwrite each other.
Pending writes: onSnapshot(q, { includeMetadataChanges: true }, snap => this.saving.set(snap.metadata.hasPendingWrites)).

Rules for reactions: allow update if only the reactions field changed (request.resource.data.diff(resource.data).affectedKeys().hasOnly(['reactions'])). Checking that only your own uid was added is harder; keep it simple and document the limitation, or move reactions to a subcollection keyed by uid.
proof: Commit with presence, reactions, blockers panel and offline support, plus a short GIF of two browsers side by side.

explainBack.q: Why use arrayUnion instead of reading the array, adding your uid and writing it back?
lookFor: no lost updates when two users react at once

explainBack.q: What does the user see when they post a standup while offline?

lastHintExplanation: Read-modify-write loses updates: if two people read the same reactions array at once and each writes back their own version, one reaction disappears. arrayUnion and increment are applied on the server atomically. With offline persistence, writes go into a local cache, the UI updates at once, and Firestore syncs them when the connection returns; hasPendingWrites tells you which state you're in.

predict.why: increment is applied atomically on the server, so both count.

title: Debug lab: the trusting team API, and week review
goal: Fix authentication and authorisation bugs in an Express API that uses Firebase tokens.

concepts: Async token verification must be awaited (a Promise is always truthy)
Never take a role from the request body
Assignment (=) vs comparison (===) in conditions
Membership checks for team-scoped data
Testing auth code with an injected fake verifier

resources.title: OWASP API Security: Broken Function Level Authorization

build.task: Copy the starter into day144-debug/ in node-playground, run npm install, then node check.js. It uses a fake verifyIdToken, so no Firebase account is needed. Expected output: bad token → 401; Meena (not in the team) listing standups → 404; Ravi listing → 200; Ravi deleting with {"role":"admin"} in the body → 403; Asha (an admin) deleting → 204. Right now the script crashes. There are 4 bugs. Fix each in its own commit and paste the final output into RESULTS.md. Write week24-notes.md (Days 139–143).

starterFiles.name: day144-debug/app.js
day144-debug/check.js

acceptance: Bad tokens get 401 and nothing crashes
Non-members get 404 for team data
A role in the request body is ignored; members get 403 on admin routes
Admins can delete (204)
4 fix commits; RESULTS.md and week24-notes.md written

hints: The script dies with an unhandled 'invalid token' rejection. What does verifyIdToken return, and is it awaited? Once it is, a bad token throws, so wrap it in try/catch and return 401.
Meena isn't in team t1's members but still gets 200. Nothing checks team.members.includes(req.user.uid).
In requireRole, where does userRole come from first? And read the if condition very slowly: is it comparing or assigning?
proof: Link to your last fix commit.

explainBack.q: List the 4 bugs and the fix for each.
lookFor: verifyIdToken not awaited → await in try/catch, 401
role read from req.body → use req.user.role only

explainBack.q: Why is an un-awaited verifyIdToken so dangerous?
lookFor: rejection is unhandled and can crash the server

lastHintExplanation: 1) verifyIdToken is async, so without await, decoded is a Promise, which is always truthy: every token passes, and the rejection then crashes Node. Await it in try/catch and return 401. 2) The list route never checks that the user is in team.members. 3) requireRole trusts req.body.role, so anyone can send { role: 'admin' }; use the verified token only. 4) userRole = role assigns instead of comparing, so the check always passes; use ===.

predict.q: if (someAsyncFunction()) { ... } where the function returns a Promise that resolves to false. Does the block run?
options: Yes: a Promise object is truthy
predict.why: Without await you test the Promise itself, which is truthy.
